M3: Under a Gaussian fit, about 0.135\% of the cells would retain data for less than this period. The 1000-point Monte Carlo simulation of~\cite{levi2026gainp} does not resolve this tail. Refreshing at $\mu-6\sigma=30.25$~$\mu$s would raise the refresh overhead of the 20-clause ALeRCE FPTM from \hyp{1.4\%} to \hyp{2.5\%} at the conservative corner. This lies within the $10\times$ sensitivity case of Section~\ref{sec:sens}.
M6: The store is 1024 bits wide and is read ahead through a prefetch buffer. The highest average demand of any model is 15.6 reads per cycle, about half the width. A strict or vanilla clause needs all its literals before its single COMPARE. The longest clause has 288 literals in the strict models and 2,004 literals in the vanilla TM models. We assume a prefetch buffer large enough that the store does not stall the array. Its area and energy are not modelled.
CPU:
We implemented three single-threaded Numba kernels.
The dense kernel packs the input into 64-bit words and counts the failing literals of a clause with population counts.
The sparse kernel walks the literal list of each clause and stops once the clause score is zero.
The bit-sliced kernel packs 64 samples into each 64-bit word. For strict and vanilla models, it ANDs the literal words of a clause and stops when no sample remains. For FPTM models, it keeps a vertical binary miss counter per clause.
Every kernel reproduced the software reference on every test sample of all 80 runs.
Every kernel within $1.5\times$ of the fastest pilot run was timed as the median of five repetitions over the full test set, each lasting at least 0.5~s. The timing includes input packing. We ran two independent passes over all runs and report, for each run, the fastest kernel of the faster pass.
The dense kernel was the fastest for all FPTM runs except the three runs of the 100-clause ALeRCE model, and the bit-sliced kernel for all strict and vanilla runs.
Both passes ran on the same virtual machine, which reported the same processor model. Because the virtual machine is shared, the two passes differed by up to 33\% for the same run, relative to the faster pass, with a median of 4.4\%. The standard deviations in Table~\ref{tab:cpu} therefore include timing noise.
TRAIN:
\textit{Port.} The Julia trainer processes samples in parallel threads. Our port trains sequentially.
The Numba kernel was checked against an independent NumPy implementation of Eq.~(\ref{eq:fptm}) on every test sample of every model.

\textit{Vanilla TM.} We use the package defaults of \texttt{pyTsetlinMachine}: 8-bit states, \texttt{boost\_true\_positive\_feedback}$\,=1$ and no literal limit.
With boosting, the reward of true literals in a firing clause is already deterministic, as in FPTM modification~2.

\textit{FPTM settings.} The FPTM specificity divisor $S$ was set once per dataset before the first training round and was not changed afterwards. It grows with the input width, so that $d=\mathrm{round}(F/S)$ is 10, 6 and 2 on WOS-46985, ALeRCE and NSL-KDD.
The FPTM models use an include limit of 200, as in two of the reference examples (MNIST and Amazon Sales)~\cite{hnilov2025code}. The $\LF=1$ models use 128, the midpoint of the 256 automaton states and the classic TM include threshold.

\textit{Seeds and stopping.} For the vanilla TM, the seed sets the C library random generator and the order of the training samples.
All strict ALeRCE runs reached the 50-epoch limit, with their best epoch between 44 and 50. Over their last 10 epochs, their best validation accuracy rose by at most 0.25 points.

\textit{Vanilla TM class sums.} The package clips each class sum to $[-T,T]$ before the argmax, whereas the exported clause set does not. The two predictions agree on at least 99.93\% of the test samples of every vanilla run.
EVAL:
To check several samples at once in Mapping~C, the simulator replicates the clause array once per sample. This is functionally equivalent to processing the samples one after another.
In Mapping~C, the vote reduction outside the array is performed in NumPy.
REFR:
One refresh reads and rewrites all 256 gain-cell rows of every occupied subarray in lockstep. It uses the local sense amplifiers of each subarray, with the bitline join open (Section~\ref{sec:mapS}). The controller starts a refresh only after a WRITE, when the tag holds no partial result. A refresh stalls the array for 512 cycles. It costs two cell operations per CAM cell, one read and one write, each charged as one CAM-cell operation. Its time and energy are amortized over the operations executed in the refresh period.}
The \gainp{} article notes that, with logical address remapping, cells in arithmetic-heavy AP operation are rewritten about every 1.2~$\mu$s on average, so that periodic refresh is mostly redundant. It nevertheless keeps refresh, conservatively~\cite{levi2026gainp}. \hyp{Here, the input rows of Mapping~S and the model rows of Mapping~C are never rewritten during inference, so they do need refresh.
